This manuscript describes a human EEG study which aims at characterizing the neural correlates of visual disappearance during perceptual filling-in (PFI) using steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP). The authors report that target disappearance leads in this paradigm to an increase rather than to a decreased SNR of the target SSVEP. The authors interpret this "neural correlate of invisibility" as an empirical challenge for existing theories regarding the relationship between SSVEP and conscious perception. The two reviewers have found the study to be creative and its findings to be of potential importance for the field. However, they have also raised concerns regarding the interpretation of the findings proposed by the authors, which would require additional analyses to be supported by the data and a more extensive account of the existing literature on the relationship between the neural correlates of visual awareness and attention. There are also concerns regarding the number of subjects included in the analyses which should be clarified. The paragraphs below describe the main concerns that have been discussed among reviewers and the reviewing editor, and that should be addressed explicitly in a revised version of the manuscript.

Essential revisions:

1) Novelty of the findings. Although the findings are interesting and novel in this particular context of perceptual filling-in, they may not be as surprising as the authors present them to be. Indeed, previous work (including some cited by the authors, e.g., Morgan, Hansen and Hillyard, 1996) has shown a clear connection between SSVEP and attention. And it is also known from previous work that PFI increases with attention (Lou, 1999; De Weerd, Smith and Greenberg, 2006). The present finding adds to this existing body of work by showing that when PFI (a "visual disappearance" effect) is used to dissociate awareness and attention, SSVEP follows attention rather than consciousness. In other words, rather than showing that SSVEP is a general neural measure of invisibility, an alternative interpretation of the finding is that SSVEP is a neural measure of attention, which in this particular setting of frequency-tagged PFI becomes a neural measure of invisibility (see also the second concern below).

2) The Abstract and the Discussion should be revised in a way that considers the finding beyond the specific context of PFI used in this study. For example, the suggestion that the "brain actively represents disappearing, or absent stimuli" should be accompanied by the alternative interpretation that SSVEP reflects a neural measure of attention rather than awareness, which in the particular setting of PFI go in opposite directions. Also, as raised by reviewer #1, previous work has studied the dissociation between the neural correlates of visual attention and awareness (among others, see e.g. Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008; 2009; Koivisto et al., 2009; Norman et al., 2013). A deeper review of the existing literature on this topic (in the Introduction and/or Discussion) would afford to better understand what is already known and also to provide insights for future work.

3) Nature of the relation between SSVEP/alpha power and attention. The authors ground their interpretation on previous studies (Lou, 1999; De Weerd et al., 2006) where attending to target features increased PFI probability, and also on the correlation they found between target-tagged SNR and alpha power. However, these are both indirect evidence – in the case of alpha power, it amounts to reverse inference to assign changes in alpha power to changes in attention. And attention was not directly manipulated in the present study, which would have provided a much stronger monitoring of the relation between attention and awareness (see, e.g., Morgan et al., 1996 or Müller et al., 2006). We thus suggest the authors to be more cautious regarding the interpretations that they seek to draw regarding attention in their study. Attention was not manipulated experimentally, and using alpha power as a measure of attention amounts to reverse inference.

4) Specificity of the finding. These results presented in the manuscript do not demonstrate that all sensory-cortical activity goes along with attention instead of awareness, as the authors' Abstract/significance statement/Discussion suggest to be the case ("by showing that the strength of stimulus-specific neural activity can encode the conscious absence of a stimulus", or "we found that neural activity increased […] when targets became invisible"). In Abstract and significance statement, the authors only state "neural activity" or "neural response", instead of SSVEP, which can be misleading. Similarly, in the Discussion, the authors should note that it remains entirely possible that other types of neural activity (e.g. spike rate or recurrent activity) in visual cortex correlates with the vividness of conscious experience, which would in principle be consistent with existing theories of visual awareness (e.g., GNW).

5) Comparison between PFI and phenomenally matched disappearances (PMD). To better characterize the difference between the responses to PFI vs. to PMD, and support the claim that target-tagged SNR decreases rather than increases during PMD (subsection “Increased SNR during invisibility is unique to targets during PFI”), it would be very important to show the target-tagged SNR changes around button press for PMD – i.e. the equivalent of Figure 2B and E for PMD.

6) Neural mechanisms underlying the observed findings. Almost no discussion about the neural mechanisms underlying the surprising finding is provided. It seems important to better explain the cortical processes involved (e.g., the authors could compare more carefully their results with those obtained in macaque electrophysiology by De Weerd et al., 1995). At the analytical level, one possibility would also be to analyse the SSVEP SNR at the intermodulation frequencies (I see in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 that responses at F2 minus F1 = 5Hz are significantly above noise). This would permit to characterize and discuss the interactions between the neural responses corresponding to the processing of the targets and to those corresponding to the processing of the surround (see e.g. Appelbaum et al., 2008).

7) Analysis of SNR change latencies. The analysis of SNR change latencies (currently described in the supplements) would deserve to be more documented and to appear in the main document. The finding that changes in background SNR precede changes in target SNR is an important result which clarifies the temporal sequence of neural activations. It would be interesting to determine when the SNR change corresponding to the inter-modulation product (e.g., at F2 minus F1) appears (see the previous concern).

8) Relation between duration of PFI and SSVEP. In the Discussion, the authors mention: "As more targets disappeared and presumably drew attention, both the duration of their absence and strength of target SNR increased." However, the duration effect, shown in supplementary materials, is not referenced in the main text. In Figure 2, in addition to investigating the relation of SSVEP with the number of disappeared targets, the authors should also test the relation of the same neural measure with the duration of PFI – or remove this sentence from the Discussion.

Reviewer #1:

In this paper, Davidson et al. characterize the neural correlates of visual disappearance during perceptual filling-in (PFI) using steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs). They show that target disappearance actually leads to an increase rather than to a decrease of the target SNR. This finding is potentially of importance and the study might ultimately lead to a publication in eLife. However, the current version of the manuscript does not provide enough details regarding the underlying assumptions and neural mechanisms. The results should also be better described, interpreted and compared to the existing literature. I list my most substantive concerns below.

1) I was a bit frustrated to see that almost no discussion about the neural mechanisms underlying the results is provided. It seems important to better explain the cortical processes involved (e.g. the authors could compare more carefully their results with those obtained in macaque electrophysiology by De Weerd et al., 1995).To go further along this direction, one possibility would also be to analyse the SNRs at the intermodulation frequencies (I see in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 that responses at F2-F1 = 5Hz are significantly above noise). This would permit to characterize and discuss the interactions between the neural responses corresponding to the processing of the targets and to the surround (see e.g. Appelbaum et al., 2008).

2) When I read the whole manuscript, I had the feeling that the analysis of the SNR change latencies (which is currently described in the supplements) would deserve to be more documented and to appear in the main document. The finding that changes in background SNR precede changes in target SNR is an important result which clarifies the temporal sequence of neural activations. That would also be nice if the authors could determine when the SNR change corresponding to the inter-modulation product (e.g. at F2-F1) appears (see my first point above).

3) To better characterize the difference between the responses to PFI vs. to phenomenally matched disappearances (PMD) and support the claim that target-SNR decreases rather than increases during PMD (subsection “Increased SNR during invisibility is unique to targets during PFI”), that would be great to show the target-SNR changes around button press (i.e. the equivalent of Figure 2B and E) for PMD.

4) The target disappearance during PFI is associated with an increase of SNR and therefore, SSVEPs in this case do not reflect conscious perception. But does it necessarily imply that this target-SNR increase reflects attention instead? The authors base their interpretation on previous studies (Lou, 1999; De Weerd et al., 2006) where attending to target feature increased PFI probability (which I think is not exactly equivalent to the PFI magnitude reported here) and also on the correlation they found between target-SNR and evoked alpha. However, these are indirect evidences and in their experimental protocol, attention was not directly manipulated (as e.g. in Morgan et al., 1996 or Müller et al., 2006). I would suggest being a little bit more cautious with this interpretation in the manuscript.

5) Before this study, other groups looked at the dissociation between attention and perceptual awareness (among others, see e.g. Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008; 2009; Koivisto et al., 2009; Norman et al., 2013). A deeper review of the existing literature on this topic (in the Introduction and/or Discussion) would permit to better understand what is already known and also to provide leads for future investigations.

Reviewer #2:

Overall, I think this is a creative study, with very interesting findings. A major weakness is that the interpretations seem a bit exaggerated and alternative interpretations not considered. Using a creative paradigm of perceptual filling-in, the authors show that increased attention (indexed by a reduction in alpha power over central-parietal locations, and supported by previous psychophysics studies) is associated with perceptual filling-in, and the phenomenal disappearance of targets. By tagging targets and surround with different frequencies, they show that SSVEP elicited by targets increases at the time of perceptual filling-in. These results suggest that SSVEP, thought to index the content of visual perception in previous binocular rivalry studies, can be dissociated from conscious perception in this paradigm, and instead reflect attention.

While the results are interesting and novel, they are perhaps not as surprising as the authors present them to be. Given that previous studies have shown a clear connection between SSVEP and attention (e.g. Morgan, Hansen and Hillyard, 1996, cited by the authors), these results shown that when attention and awareness are dissociated (as the last author has nicely demonstrated/argued previously), SSVEP goes with attention.

These results do not demonstrate that all sensory-cortical activity goes along with attention instead of awareness, as the authors' Abstract/significance statement/Discussion suggest to be the case. E.g., in Abstract/significance statement, the authors only state "neural activity" or "neural response", instead of specifically SSVEP, which can be misleading. Similarly, in the Discussion, it remains a possibility that other types of neural activity (e.g. spiking rate or recurrent activity) in sensory cortex correlates with the vividness of conscious experience, which would in principle be consistent with first-order or GNW theories.

An analysis comment:

In the Discussion, the authors mention "As more targets disappeared and presumably drew attention, both the duration of their absence and strength of target SNR increased." The duration effect, shown in supplementary materials, is not referenced in the main text as I as I could find. In Figure 2, in addition to investigating SSVEP's relation with the number of disappeared targets, the authors could also test its relation with the duration of PFI.

claims.evidence: Direct statement about prior study findings with citation.

claims.claim: Directing attention toward targets in the visual periphery facilitates perceptual disappearance during PFI.

claims.claim: PFI occurs regularly in normal vision, as in the visual areas that are occluded by the blindspot, and the blood vessels in the retina.

claims.evidence: Direct statement about PFI occurrence with citations.

claims.evidence: Direct statement about IM components with citations.

results.result: The study recruited 19 healthy adults (12 females, 19-40 years, M=26.95, SD=7.63) via convenience sampling from Monash University students, with appropriate exclusion criteria and ethics approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide complete demographic and procedural information about participant recruitment. The sample characteristics, recruitment method, compensation, exclusion criteria, and ethics approval are all explicitly documented, meeting standard reporting requirements for human subjects research.

results.result: The experimental apparatus consisted of a dynamic texture display with frequency-tagged targets (15 Hz) and surrounds (20 Hz), with individually calibrated target eccentricity to optimize both PFI occurrence and SSVEP strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C17 comprehensively describe the stimulus apparatus and calibration procedure. The specifications are detailed and internally consistent, including monitor parameters, stimulus characteristics, and the novel dynamic texture tagging method. The individual calibration approach (C17) addresses the known trade-off between SSVEP strength and PFI occurrence.

results.result: EEG was recorded using 64 active electrodes arranged according to the international 10-10 system, with impedances kept below 10 kΩ, sampled at 1000 Hz with offline bandpass filtering of 0.5-70 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 provide standard and complete EEG acquisition parameters. The electrode configuration, impedance threshold, sampling rate, and filtering parameters are all within accepted ranges for SSVEP research and are clearly documented.

results.result: Target eccentricity was calibrated per participant from 4.3° to 8.7° in 0.4° steps based on subjective reports and real-time SSVEP monitoring, with all participants reporting PFI occurrence.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 describe the calibration procedure with appropriate detail. The range of eccentricities, adjustment steps, and dual criteria (subjective PFI reports and SSVEP strength) are clearly specified. The acknowledgment that tagging was unsuccessful for 2 participants (C24) demonstrates transparency in reporting.

results.result: Participants completed 48 one-minute trials reporting target visibility via four keyboard buttons, with embedded phenomenally matched disappearance (PMD) periods (3.5-5 s duration) occurring after the first 10 seconds of each trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 provide complete experimental procedure details. The response mapping, trial structure, break schedule, and PMD implementation are all clearly specified. The PMD timing rationale (C30) is supported by appropriate citation, and the decision not to inform participants about PMD (C29) is a reasonable methodological choice to maintain ecological validity.

results.result: Three participants were excluded for failing to detect PMD periods, with the remaining 16 participants showing a mean PMD detection reaction time of 0.68 s (SD=0.31), and only 16 trials rejected across all retained participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 document participant exclusion and task performance with appropriate statistical detail. The exclusion criteria based on PMD detection is reasonable for ensuring task engagement. The low trial rejection rate (C34) indicates good data quality. The observation about button release behavior (C32) shows careful data inspection.

results.result: Targets disappeared together more frequently than in isolation, and PFI duration increased with the number of invisible targets, replicating prior findings of facilitatory grouping mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report behavioral findings consistent with prior work (C36 cites Davidson et al., 2020). While the claims reference supplementary results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the replication of established phenomena and citation of prior work support these findings. However, the main text lacks detailed statistical support for these behavioral claims.

results.result: During PFI, target-specific neural responses (target-SNR) increased prior to subjective reports of target invisibility, showing a significant negative correlation with conscious perception (pcluster<0.001 from -0.74s to 1.53s; χ²(1)=11.60, p=6.58×10⁻⁴).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 present the core counterintuitive finding with appropriate statistical support. The cluster-based permutation test (C38) and linear mixed-effects model (C40) are appropriate analyses. The temporal window and effect direction are clearly specified. The finding directly contradicts the typical interpretation of SSVEPs as consciousness correlates.

results.result: Surround-SNR tracked phenomenology during PFI, increasing during target disappearance (pcluster<0.001 from -0.99s to 1.28s; χ²(1)=19.63, p=9.41×10⁻⁶), and positively correlating with both target-SNR and the number of invisible targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 demonstrate that surround-SNR behaves as expected for a consciousness correlate, contrasting with target-SNR. The statistical support is robust with both cluster-based and linear mixed-effects analyses. The positive correlation between target and surround signals (C43) is critical for the attention interpretation.

results.result: During PMD (physical target removal), target-SNR decreased (χ²(1)=18.35, p=1.84×10⁻⁵) while surround-SNR increased (χ²(1)=7.37, p=0.007), demonstrating that increased target-SNR during invisibility is specific to endogenously generated PFI.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 provide the critical control comparison showing that the paradoxical target-SNR increase is specific to PFI and not a general response to target invisibility. The opposite pattern during PMD (target-SNR decreases) strongly supports the interpretation that the PFI effect reflects attention rather than visibility. Statistical support is robust.

results.result: Alpha amplitude showed significant event-related suppression during PFI (pcluster=0.004, -0.14s to 0.65s, p<0.011 FDR-corrected) in centro-parietal electrodes, but not during PMD after FDR correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 document alpha suppression during PFI using appropriate cluster-based permutation tests with FDR correction. The spatial (centro-parietal) and temporal specificity are clearly reported. The lack of significant PMD effect after correction (C51) strengthens the interpretation that alpha suppression is specific to endogenous PFI processes.

results.result: Across participants, evoked alpha suppression negatively correlated with target-SNR strength during PFI (r=-0.58, p=0.019) but not during PMD (r=-0.34, p=0.22).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 provide correlational evidence linking alpha suppression (an attention marker) to target-SNR increases during PFI. The correlation is moderate and statistically significant for PFI but not PMD, supporting the attention interpretation. However, with N=16, the correlation should be interpreted cautiously, and the lack of correction for multiple comparisons is a minor concern.

results.result: During PFI, surround-SNR changes preceded target-SNR changes by approximately 200 ms, with jackknife analysis confirming this temporal order was consistent across all subsamples (t(15)=9.36, p=1.94×10⁻⁷).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 establish the temporal sequence of neural events during PFI using appropriate jackknife resampling. The 200 ms lag is clearly specified, and the statistical support is robust. The consistency across all jackknifed subsamples (C57) demonstrates the reliability of this temporal ordering, which has important mechanistic implications.

results.result: Intermodulation (IM) SNR changes occurred between surround and target SNR changes (median=-0.83s, SD=0.09), though this was less statistically reliable with no significant cluster retained on 43% of jackknifed subsamples.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 report IM timing but acknowledge limited reliability. The 43% failure rate in jackknife subsamples (C58) indicates this finding is not robust, attributed to weak IM-SNR strength. While the median timing falls between surround and target as predicted, the statistical uncertainty prevents strong conclusions about IM component involvement in PFI mechanisms.

results.result: During PMD, the temporal pattern reversed with target-SNR changes preceding surround-SNR changes (t(15)=-16.64, p=4.48×10⁻¹¹), and IM-SNR changes occurring after button press, while target-SNR latencies were equivalent between PFI and PMD conditions (t(15)=-1.56, p=0.14).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 demonstrate a complete reversal of temporal dynamics during PMD compared to PFI, with robust statistical support. The equivalent target-SNR latencies between conditions (C63) suggests the target response is time-locked to the report rather than the perceptual event, while the reversed surround-target sequence during PMD supports distinct mechanisms for endogenous versus exogenous disappearances.

results.result: EEG preprocessing included modified PREP pipeline (omitting bad-by-RANSAC), spherical interpolation of bad channels (M=5.70, SD=0.62), re-referencing to average, linear detrending, downsampling to 250 Hz, and Laplacian transform.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C177 document standard EEG preprocessing steps with appropriate justification for modifications. The omission of bad-by-RANSAC (C173-C174) is well-justified given that frequency-tagging produces localized, correlated responses. The preprocessing pipeline is comprehensive and appropriate for SSVEP analysis.

results.result: Rhythmic entrainment source separation (RESS) was applied to create optimized spatial filters for each frequency of interest, using data from -3000 to -100 ms and 100 to 3000 ms around button press/release, avoiding motor-evoked activity and condition-specific overfitting.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C186 describe the RESS analysis method with appropriate detail and justification. The rationale for using RESS given topographic variability (C178) is sound. The filter construction procedure (C183-C185) shows careful consideration of potential confounds (motor activity, overfitting). RESS is an appropriate method for maximizing SNR in frequency-tagged responses.

results.result: Four convergent lines of evidence support the interpretation that SSVEP strength reflects attention rather than consciousness during PFI: (1) targets sharing features disappear together suggesting attentional grouping, (2) alpha suppression indicates attention increases during PFI but not PMD, (3) target-SNR correlates with alpha suppression during PFI, and (4) IM-SNR increases transiently during PFI consistent with multi-object attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C112 synthesize multiple lines of evidence into a coherent interpretation. Each line of evidence is individually supported by data presented in the manuscript. The convergence of behavioral (C98-C100), alpha-band (C101-C103), correlational (C104), and IM (C105-C107) evidence strengthens the attention interpretation. The explicit consideration and rejection of alternative explanations (C109-C110) demonstrates rigorous reasoning. However, the evidence is largely correlational and indirect.

results.result: The temporal sequence during PFI (surround-SNR → IM-SNR → target-SNR) with approximately 200 ms between surround and target changes provides evidence for neural interactions between target and background representations during filling-in.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116, C120 establish a temporal sequence that has mechanistic implications for PFI. The consistency across participants (C115) and the intermediate timing of IM components (C116) support interaction-based models of PFI. However, the interpretation relies on assumptions about what IM components represent, and the IM finding itself was noted as less reliable (C58).

results.result: The temporal ordering of surround, IM, and target activations challenges models claiming interactions between stimulus representations are unnecessary for PFI, though the dynamic texture design may reduce boundary adaptation and shift the neural correlates to higher visual areas like V4.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 discuss implications for PFI models but acknowledge important caveats. While the temporal ordering (C82) does challenge certain models, the authors appropriately note that their stimulus design (C83) may reduce boundary adaptation, potentially changing which neural mechanisms are engaged. The speculation about V4 involvement (C84) is reasonable but unsupported by direct evidence.

results.result: The finding that target SSVEP strength increases during invisibility challenges theories proposing response strength positively correlates with conscious experience, though the exact mechanisms of SSVEP generation remain poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 appropriately qualify the theoretical implications. The challenge to first-order and GNWT theories (C87) is valid given the data, but the caveat about SSVEP generation mechanisms (C88) is important. The authors correctly note that the relationship between scalp-recorded SSVEPs and underlying neural spiking is not fully understood, limiting strong theoretical conclusions.

results.result: This study is the first to demonstrate a neural correlate of the counterintuitive opposing effects of attention and consciousness, showing that SSVEP strength during PFI reflects attention rather than conscious perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C128, C134-C135, C142-C143, C156 state the main conclusion with appropriate support from the convergent evidence presented. The novelty claim (C128) appears justified as prior SSVEP studies confounded attention and consciousness. The conclusion that SSVEPs reflect attention (C143) is supported by indirect but convergent evidence (C135). However, the evidence is correlational and the interpretation relies on assumptions about alpha and IM components.

results.result: Prior research has interpreted SSVEP strength as a neural correlate of consciousness during binocular rivalry and as a measure of attention in other contexts, but these interpretations may be confounded, with a more parsimonious explanation being that SSVEPs primarily reflect attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68, C131-C133 accurately summarize prior literature with extensive citations. The observation that SSVEPs have been used to measure both consciousness and attention in different contexts (C64-C67) is well-documented. The critique of Zhang et al. (2011) interpretation (C132) and the alternative parsimonious explanation (C133) are reasonable given the current findings, though this represents a reinterpretation rather than definitive proof.

results.result: Prior single-unit recordings during binocular rivalry in macaques showed that half of responsive neurons (22% of recorded neurons in V4 and MT) exhibited enhanced firing when their preferred stimulus was suppressed, providing precedent for negative correlations between neural activity and visibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 accurately cite prior work (Logothetis, 1998; Logothetis, 1989a; Logothetis and Schall, 1989b) showing neurons can increase firing during perceptual suppression. This provides important context that the current finding, while counterintuitive, has precedent. The interpretation (C91) that this counters simple activity-consciousness correlations is appropriate.

results.result: The findings demonstrate the need to re-examine previous uses of SSVEPs as consciousness correlates and position dynamic texture tagging as a promising method for future consciousness research, potentially using no-report paradigms to further dissociate attention and consciousness.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C138-C139 appropriately discuss implications and future directions. The call to re-examine prior SSVEP interpretations (C96) is justified by the current findings. The methodological contribution of dynamic texture tagging (C97, C138) is valid. The suggestion for future no-report studies (C139) is reasonable, though speculative.

results.result: PFI is characterized by attention facilitating target disappearance, occurs regularly in normal vision, and has been proposed as a promising paradigm to dissociate neural correlates of attention and consciousness.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C151-C155 accurately characterize PFI based on prior literature with appropriate citations. The unusual property that attention facilitates disappearance (C69) is well-established. The occurrence in normal vision (C70) and the proposal as a dissociation paradigm (C155) are appropriately cited. These claims provide important context for the study rationale.

results.result: The study predicted that if SSVEPs reflect visibility, target and surround signals should anti-correlate during PFI, but if SSVEPs reflect attention, these signals should positively correlate as attention to a location would enhance both target and surround responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C171 clearly state the competing predictions that motivated the study design. These predictions are logically derived from the properties of PFI and the dual interpretations of SSVEPs. The data support the attention prediction (positive correlation), providing strong evidence for the study's main conclusion.
